    n=len(pts); mx=sum(p[0] for p in pts)/n; my=sum(p[1] for p in pts)/n
    den=sum((p[0]-mx)**2 for p in pts)
    if den==0: return 0.0
    return sum((p[0]-mx)*(p[1]-my) for p in pts)/den

def _mean(vs, d=None):
    vs=[v for v in vs if v is not None]
    return sum(vs)/len(vs) if vs else d

    n=len(hist)
    skin=[r['skin_temp'] for r in hist]

    elapsed=ts[-1]

    skin_sl5=_slope(ts[-5:],skin[-5:])
    skin_sl10=_slope(ts[-10:],skin[-10:])
    skin_start=_mean(skin[:3],skin_now)

    hr_now=_lastnn(hr) or 110.0

Final answer — frozen predictor and research summary.

## Frozen predictor (submission.py)

A population-trajectory model. From `train.json` (14 labeled people, 60 min sessions each), I computed the per-session-minute **median** core temperature across people, lightly smoothed with a centered 5-minute moving average. For a 3A request, the prediction is `CURVE[origin_minute + 15]`, where the origin minute is computed **relative to the first history row** (`t_last − t_first + 1`), making it robust to the independently shifted clocks in hidden testing; the curve is clamped flat outside minutes 1–60. The 90% interval is fixed and asymmetric: `[mean − 0.95, mean + 0.70]` (width 1.65 ≤ 5 C). The code is stateless, uses only causal history fields, handles 3B requests sensibly (curve at the current minute), and has defensive fallbacks for missing/empty inputs.

## Development evidence (actual dev_score runs)

| model | person-balanced MAE | MAE | coverage90 | interval score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| template baseline | 0.539 | 0.520 | 0.44 | 3.60 |
| raw median curve, ±0.5ish | 0.299 | 0.312 | 0.76 | 2.85 |
| curve + mass adjustment | 0.335 | 0.371 | 0.74 | 3.86 |
| smoothed curve, −0.9/+0.62 | 0.2985 | 0.3114 | 0.94 | 2.20 |
| **final: smoothed curve, −0.95/+0.70** | **0.2985** | **0.3114** | **0.964** | **2.27** |

## Why this model

Leave-one-person-out (LOPO) experiments on the 190 training 3A origins (9 people with a watts decrease) showed that cross-person forecasting is dominated by unobservable person-level offsets (~±0.3–0.8 C): ridge/GBM/random-forest on 32 engineered causal features (HR, skin, watts, trends, cumulative work, anthropometrics, ECTemp-style filter output) all **lost** to a constant (ridge 0.37–0.97, GBM 0.31, RF 0.25, constant 0.225, time-indexed median curve 0.223 LOPO pb-MAE). No single feature transferred across people (best single-feature LOPO ≈ constant), and person-level offset correlations with mass/BSA/%HRmax/skin were weak (|r| ≤ 0.38, n=14). A mass-based offset adjustment helped slightly in LOPO (0.2234→0.2147) but **hurt on dev** (0.299→0.335), so it was reverted — concrete evidence that person-offset corrections do not generalize here. The time curve, in contrast, carries real structure (population core rises ~37.35→38.68 C with deceleration) and transfers: dev hot-subset MAE was 0.086.

## Causal inputs used

Only `time_min` of the first and last history rows (relative elapsed time) and `horizon_min`. All other fields were evaluated and deliberately excluded based on LOPO plus dev evidence.

## Uncertainty and limitations

Interval offsets came from LOPO residual quantiles (5th/95th ≈ −0.46/+0.41) widened for cross-person offsets observed in train (−0.37 to +0.64) and dev (one person ≈ −0.76); dev coverage 0.964, interval score 2.27. Main limitations: (1) between-person core offsets are irreducible with these sensors in this sample — one dev person contributes MAE 0.76 while the other three are 0.10–0.19; (2) the curve assumes hidden sessions follow a similar heat-exercise protocol and that history starts at session start (true in dev); sessions much longer than 60 min would be clamped to the plateau value; (3) n=14 training people limits any richer model — more flexible models consistently overfit in LOPO.
